title: Bring Your Own Model to the GitHub Copilot SDK with C#
summary: The GitHub Copilot SDK gives your application an agent runtime. BYOK lets you keep that runtime while sending model requests to your own Microsoft Foundry or Azure OpenAI deployment. Here is the complete C# setup. The post Bring Your Own Model to the GitHub Copilot SDK with C# appeared first on .NET Blog .
content:
Hi,

I know, I keep coming back to the same theme on this blog: **agent harnesses**. In [Build Your Own AI Agent Harness in C#](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/build-your-own-ai-agent-harness-in-csharp-the-maf-claw-live-series/) we built one from scratch. In [From dotnet run to Foundry Hosted Agent in 3 lines of C#](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/from-dotnet-run-to-foundry-hosted-agent-in-3-lines-of-csharp/) we took an agent and hosted it. Today we use a harness we do not have to build at all: the one GitHub already ships, through the **GitHub Copilot SDK**.

One of the most popular questions we received during the **Let’s Learn GitHub Copilot SDK** sessions was:

> “Can I use the Copilot SDK with my own model deployment?”

The short answer is **yes**.

The longer answer is, the GitHub Copilot SDK gives your application the Copilot agent runtime, while `ProviderConfig` lets you route model inference to a provider you control. That provider can be any of the [providers officially supported by the Copilot SDK](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/auth/byok): OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Microsoft Foundry Local, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as vLLM or LiteLLM. Today’s sample uses **Microsoft Foundry**, authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID or, when needed, an API key.

The complete sample is now part of [Generative AI for Beginners .NET](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK). It is a small .NET 10 console application: read configuration, create a BYOK provider, start the Copilot runtime, create one session, and ask one question.

[Get the complete BYOK C# sample](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK)

## What BYOK means in this sample

BYOK means **Bring Your Own Key**, but in this context the important idea is broader than the key itself: you bring your own model provider.

The Copilot SDK still supplies the runtime that manages the client, session, system message, and agent configuration. `ProviderConfig` changes the destination and authentication for model inference.

**BYOK is not customer-managed encryption keys**

In this article, BYOK means using your own model endpoint and credentials for inference. It does not refer to customer-managed encryption keys or a storage-encryption configuration.

The sample intentionally keeps the session minimal. It disables tools, skills, configuration discovery, and host Git operations so that the first run demonstrates one thing clearly: a Copilot SDK session can send a model request to your own Foundry-compatible deployment.

![Diagram of a .NET app routing Copilot SDK requests to Microsoft Foundry](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/feed/github-copilot-sdk-byok-diagram.svg)

*The runtime and the model provider are separate parts of the application.*

## The project

The sample is a regular .NET 10 console application. These are the packages it uses:

```
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <UserSecretsId>genai-beginners-dotnet</UserSecretsId>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Azure.Identity" Version="1.21.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="GitHub.Copilot.SDK" Version="1.0.11" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration" Version="10.0.3" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.UserSecrets" Version="10.0.3" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

`GitHub.Copilot.SDK` provides the .NET client for the Copilot runtime. `Azure.Identity` provides `AzureCliCredential`, which lets the sample reuse the identity from `az login`. The configuration packages load development-only secrets without putting endpoints or credentials in source control.

## Step 1: read the model configuration

The sample uses the shared User Secrets values already used by the repository:

```
// User Secrets keeps the endpoint and credentials outside the repository.
var configuration = new ConfigurationBuilder()
    .AddUserSecrets<Program>(optional: true)
    .Build();

// This sample uses the repo's shared AzureOpenAI secrets.
var modelName = GetRequiredValue(configuration, "AzureOpenAI:Deployment");
var endpoint = GetRequiredValue(configuration, "AzureOpenAI:Endpoint");
var apiKey = configuration["AzureOpenAI:ApiKey"]?.Trim();
```

There are two required values:

* `AzureOpenAI:Deployment` is the name of your model deployment in Microsoft Foundry or Azure OpenAI. Choose a deployment that supports the Responses API, because this sample uses `WireApi = "responses"`.
* `AzureOpenAI:Endpoint` is the Foundry or Azure OpenAI resource endpoint.

`AzureOpenAI:ApiKey` is optional. If it is not present, the sample uses Microsoft Entra ID through `AzureCliCredential`. If it is present, the sample sends it in the `api-key` header.

## Step 2: configure the provider

This is the core of the sample:

```
// Microsoft Foundry exposes an API compatible with OpenAI Responses.
var provider = new ProviderConfig
{
    Type = "openai",
    BaseUrl = NormalizeEndpoint(endpoint),
    WireApi = "responses",
    ModelId = modelName,
    WireModel = modelName,
    MaxPromptTokens = 8000,
    MaxOutputTokens = 512
};
```

The configuration tells the Copilot runtime how to communicate with the provider:

* `Type = "openai"` selects the OpenAI-compatible provider shape.
* `BaseUrl` points to the OpenAI-compatible API surface.
* `WireApi = "responses"` selects the Responses API.
* `ModelId` identifies the model to the Copilot runtime.
* `WireModel` is the model name sent to the provider.
* The token limits keep this small example bounded.

For a reasoning model, `MaxOutputTokens` includes reasoning tokens as well as the visible answer. The 512-token limit can be reached before the model produces any answer. Increase or omit the `MaxOutputTokens` override when using a reasoning deployment, then tune the limit for your workload.

In this sample, `ModelId` and `WireModel` have the same value. They are separate properties because the runtime-facing model identifier and the provider-facing model name do not have to be identical in every integration.

The endpoint helper accepts either the resource URL or a URL that already includes `/openai/v1/`:

```
static string NormalizeEndpoint(string endpoint)
{
    var candidate = endpoint.Trim();
    if (!Uri.TryCreate(candidate, UriKind.Absolute, out var uri) ||
        uri.Scheme != Uri.UriSchemeHttps ||
        string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(uri.Host))
    {
        throw new ArgumentException("The configured AzureOpenAI:Endpoint must be an HTTPS URL.");
    }

    // Accept the resource URL or a URL that already ends in /openai/v1.
    // Trimming first means a trailing slash does not need a separate check.
    var trimmed = candidate.TrimEnd('/');
    if (trimmed.EndsWith("/openai/v1", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
    {
        return trimmed + "/";
    }

    return $"{uri.GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority).TrimEnd('/')}/openai/v1/";
}
```

The helper also requires HTTPS. It is better to reject a malformed endpoint before creating a session than to discover it after the first model request.

## Step 3: use Entra ID by default

The default authentication path uses the Azure CLI login:

```
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(apiKey))
{
    // AzureCliCredential reuses the session created with `az login`.
    var credential = new AzureCliCredential();
    var scope = "https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default";
#pragma warning disable GHCP001 // BYOK auth callbacks are experimental in the Copilot SDK.
    provider.BearerTokenProvider = async _ =>
    {
        var token = await credential.GetTokenAsync(
            new TokenRequestContext([scope]),
            cancellation.Token);
        return token.Token;
    };
#pragma warning restore GHCP001
}
```

Before signing in, make sure your identity has the **Cognitive Services OpenAI User** role on the resource. Then run:

```
az login
```

`BearerTokenProvider` is a callback. The SDK can call it when it needs a token instead of receiving one token value that the application has to manage itself.

## Step 4: use an API key when one is configured

Some deployments or environments still require an API key. The sample supports that path without changing the rest of the provider configuration:

```
else
{
    provider.Headers = new Dictionary<string, string>
    {
        ["api-key"] = apiKey
    };
}
```

Set the optional secret:

```
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:ApiKey" "<your-api-key>"
```

When the value exists, the sample uses the `api-key` header and does not require `az login`. The console output reports only the authentication mode; it never prints the endpoint or the credential.

**Keep credentials out of source control**

Use User Secrets for local development, environment-managed configuration for deployed applications, and never paste an API key into the source file or a README.

## Step 5: start the Copilot runtime

The provider controls model inference, but the Copilot runtime is still required:

```
await using var client = new CopilotClient(new CopilotClientOptions
{
    Connection = RuntimeConnection.ForStdio("copilot"),
    WorkingDirectory = AppContext.BaseDirectory
});
await client.StartAsync(cancellation.Token);
```

This is an important distinction. BYOK does not mean “the Copilot SDK without Copilot.” The local Copilot CLI runtime still provides the orchestration process. BYOK changes where the model request goes.

**Prerequisites**

Install the .NET 10 SDK and the GitHub Copilot CLI, and make sure `dotnet --version` reports a .NET 10 SDK and `copilot --version` works. For the default Microsoft Entra ID authentication path, also install the Azure CLI and make sure `az --version` works. The API-key path does not require the Azure CLI. The sample starts the local Copilot runtime through `RuntimeConnection.ForStdio("copilot")`.

## Step 6: create a deliberately small session

The session configuration connects the model name and provider, then disables capabilities that are outside the scope of this first example:

```
// Disable tools, skills, and Git operations to isolate the model request.
await using var session = await client.CreateSessionAsync(new SessionConfig
{
    ClientName = "github-copilot-sdk-byok",
    Model = modelName,
    Provider = provider,
    SystemMessage = new SystemMessageConfig
    {
        Mode = SystemMessageMode.Replace,
        Content = "Answer every user question in English. Be concise and factual."
    },
    AvailableTools = [],
    Tools = [],
    EnableConfigDiscovery = false,
    EnableSkills = false,
    EnableHostGitOperations = false
}, cancellation.Token);
```

The empty tool collections and disabled features are intentional. They make the sample easier to reason about and safer to run while learning the provider configuration.

The system message also makes the output predictable for a multilingual live-learning sample. `SystemMessageMode.Replace` replaces the default system message instead of appending another instruction to it.

## Step 7: send one question

Finally, the application sends one prompt and waits for the final response:

```
var response = await session.SendAndWaitAsync(
    new MessageOptions { Prompt = question },
    TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3),
    cancellation.Token);

var content = response?.Data.Content;
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(content))
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException("The model returned an empty response.");
}

Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine("Answer:");
Console.WriteLine(content);
```

The default question is:

```
What is Microsoft Foundry, and how does it relate to the GitHub Copilot SDK?
```

You can provide another question as command-line arguments:

```
dotnet run -- "Explain BYOK in one sentence."
```

## Run the sample

From the sample directory, configure the required values:

```
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:Endpoint" "https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com"
dotnet user-secrets set "AzureOpenAI:Deployment" "<your-deployment-name>"
```

Then use the default Entra ID path:

```
az login
dotnet run
```

The output looks like this:

```
Model: <your-deployment-name>
Authentication: AzureCliCredential
Question: What is Microsoft Foundry, and how does it relate to the GitHub Copilot SDK?

Answer:
<model response>
```

The sample prints the selected model and authentication mode, but not the endpoint or credentials.

## So, what did we actually learn here?

Honestly, the part I like most is how little code this takes. ![🙂](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f642.png)

The Copilot SDK runtime and the model provider are two different things, and once that clicks, the rest is easy. You keep the runtime that GitHub gives you: the client, the session, the system message, and the agent plumbing. Then you just point inference somewhere else. That “somewhere else” is your Foundry deployment, your OpenAI key, your local Ollama, whatever you need.

Entra ID is the default path here, and I think it should be. No key to rotate, no key to leak, no key to accidentally commit. `az login` and you are done. The API key branch is there for the cases where you really need it, and it stays out of the way until you configure it.

And the session is deliberately boring. No tools, no skills, no MCP, no Git access. That is on purpose: the first run has exactly one job, which is proving that your model is answering. Once you see that answer in the console, you have a working baseline.

That is the fun part. From here you can start adding things one at a time: tools, MCP servers, skills, approvals, and streaming. When something breaks, you will know exactly which piece broke it.

Go try it with your own deployment. ![🚀](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/72x72/1f680.png)

[Explore the complete GitHub Copilot SDK sample](https://github.com/microsoft/Generative-AI-for-beginners-dotnet/tree/main/samples/CoreSamples/GitHubCopilotSDK-01-BYOK)

Happy coding!

Bruno

content:
Years ago, in a galaxy far, far away, my colleagues in support, Keith Elmore and Robert Dorr, built a tool called **ostress.exe**. For decades it transformed the way we reproduced customer issues for SQL Server. The engineering team used it, and up until now I've used it for demonstrations, books, and examples. Its magic was simple: ostress could simulate many concurrent users running SQL queries or scripts.

I decided to rethink ostress for today's SQL world, and the result is sqlsimtools, now in public preview at https://aka.ms/sqlsimtools. It's a free, open-source suite of workload simulation tools for SQL Server 2019, 2022, and 2025, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric. I've been building it for some time and using it at events and in demonstrations. Now I want everyone to have it.

The public preview includes:

* **sqlsim**: a native, ODBC-based command-line tool for Windows (x64 and ARM64) and Ubuntu Linux.
* **sqlpysim:** a Python version of sqlsim built on Microsoft's mssql-python driver, for Windows and Ubuntu Linux.
* **sqlsim Studio**: a self-contained local browser app that configures, runs, monitors, replays, and compares workloads using sqlsim or sqlpysim. It's available today on Windows x64.

I'm also looking for Private Preview testers for macOS, and for sqlsim Studio on Linux and Windows ARM64. If you'd like to help, request Private Preview access.

I'll be writing more posts on different parts of the tools, but here are my top 10 cool things you can do with sqlsimtools:

* Run any SQL query, script, or mixed workload
* Create your own benchmarks, load tests, and stress tests
* Configure, run, monitor, and compare workloads visually with sqlsim Studio
* Replay captured SQL Server activity
* Monitor workload performance live or after execution
* Run before-and-after experiments with detailed performance comparisons
* Test SQL Server, Azure SQL, and SQL database in Microsoft Fabric with flexible authentication
* Use native or Python tools on Windows, Linux, and macOS (Private Preview)
* Automate testing with JSON results and live event streams
* Build and run workloads with AI agents such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Cursor

Get started today at <https://aka.ms/sqlsimtools> . The easiest way to start is the all-in-one sqlsimtools package, which includes sqlsim Studio and both command-line tools. You can also download just the tool for your platform, or clone the repo and build it yourself. On Windows, unblock the ZIP before you extract it, because the tools aren't code signed.

sqlsimtools is an open-source project, not an official Microsoft product, and isn't covered by Microsoft support. For questions and ideas, join the conversation in GitHub Discussions ([microsoft/sqlsimtools · Discussions · GitHub](https://github.com/microsoft/sqlsimtools/discussions)), and report bugs in GitHub Issues ([Issues · microsoft/sqlsimtools](https://github.com/microsoft/sqlsimtools/issues)). During Public Preview I'm not taking Pull Requests yet but file issues and as the project progresses, we will incorporate the PR process.

Bob Ward

The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you *love* the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.

I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.

Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.

That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: **"Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"**

So here it is.

Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

> 📌 **A quick note:** A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

## Visitor Stats 📊

Before the tour starts, a few numbers:

* **65 authors, 65 masterpieces.**
* **600+ minutes** of listed reading time. That's over 10 hours, and in reality it was much more, because listed reading time is a polite lie.
* **The longest read:** 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100.
* **The shortest read:** 1 minute.
* **The oldest exhibit:** published in March 2020.
* **The most reactions:** 623.
* **Zero reactions:** 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists.

---

## How to Tour the Hall

The exhibits are grouped into wings by theme, so you can head straight to whatever interests you most. Each exhibit has the article itself, why the author picked it (when they told me), and my take.

* 🚪 **The Welcome Desk:** where every visitor should start
* 🏛️ **Stories From the Trenches:** careers, first steps, and the people behind the code
* 💡 **The "Finally, It Clicked" Gallery:** fundamentals explained the way they should be
* ⚙️ **The Engine Room:** systems, internals, and seriously deep dives
* 🤖 **The AI Lab:** building with AI, and finding out where it breaks
* 🧠 **The Philosophy Floor:** thinking about AI, engineering, and the craft itself
* 🔧 **The Builder's Garage:** real tools solving real problems

Grab a coffee. It's a big building.

Most agent demos have a happy path: the model picks a tool, the tool returns 200, the agent moves on. Production is different. In production, the tool call sometimes returns nothing at all.

That is where a correct decision turns into a wrong outcome.

## The gap between "decided" and "done"

Here is an illustrative scenario (not a real incident, but a very ordinary one).

An agent handles a support ticket and decides the customer is owed a refund. It calls `POST /refunds`. The payments service processes the refund, writes it to its ledger, and starts sending the response. The network hiccups. The agent's HTTP client hits its timeout and raises an error.

From the agent's point of view, the call failed. From the payment service's point of view, it succeeded. The agent's loop sees an error, and the most natural thing for it to do is try again.

Now the customer has two refunds.

The model reasoned perfectly. It picked the right action with the right arguments. Nothing about better prompting, a bigger model, or a smarter planner fixes this, because the failure happened after the reasoning was over.

## Failure mode 1: treating a timeout as a "no"

A timeout tells you one thing: you didn't get an answer. It does not tell you the action didn't happen. Agent frameworks that wrap tool errors into "the tool failed, decide what to do next" collapse three different situations into one:

* the request never reached the service
* the request reached it and was rejected
* the request reached it, succeeded, and the response was lost

Only the first two are safe to retry blindly.

## Failure mode 2: no idempotency key

If the agent had sent an idempotency key, the second refund call would have been a no-op that returned the original result. The key has to be generated by the application *before* the first attempt and reused on every retry of that same intent:

```
intent = actions.record_intent(
    kind="refund",
    order_id=order.id,
    amount=amount,
    idempotency_key=uuid4(),   # created once, stored with the intent
)

try:
    result = payments.refund(
        order_id=order.id,
        amount=amount,
        idempotency_key=intent.idempotency_key,
    )
    actions.mark_confirmed(intent.id, result)
except Timeout:
    actions.mark_unknown(intent.id)   # NOT "failed"
```

The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing.

## Failure mode 3: state that only exists in the context window

If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The intent needs to be written to durable storage before execution, so that whatever process picks the work back up can see it.

## Failure mode 4: no "outcome unknown" state

Most action models have two terminal states: success and failure. Reliable ones need at least:

* `submitted`: we sent it, no answer yet
* `confirmed`: the downstream system acknowledged it
* `failed`: the downstream system explicitly rejected it
* `unknown`: we can't tell

`unknown` is the one that matters. It's the state that should block automatic retries and trigger reconciliation instead.

## Failure mode 5: no reconciliation path

When an action lands in `unknown`, something has to go find out the truth: query the payment service by idempotency key or order ID, compare against the ledger, and then move the intent to `confirmed` or `failed`. That can be a background job, a scheduled check, or a human queue for high-value actions. What it can't be is the agent deciding "probably fine" or "probably failed" on its own.

## The reframe

Agent tool use is really remote procedure calls with an LLM choosing which procedure to call. Everything we already know about RPCs over unreliable networks still applies: idempotency, durable intent logs, explicit uncertainty, reconciliation.

The clean split is:

* **The model proposes** an action.
* **The application owns** the execution state: the key, the intent record, the status, the retry policy.

"Try again" is a fine default for reads. For anything that changes state, it's only safe once you know the first attempt didn't land, or once the downstream system guarantees a retry can't double-apply.

## Build vs. integrate

If you already run payment or order flows with idempotency keys and outbox/ledger patterns, you mostly need to route agent actions through that same machinery instead of letting the agent call APIs directly. If you don't, that's the piece to build (or adopt) first, before giving an agent write access to anything that moves money or data.

How are you handling the "we don't know if it happened" case in your agent workflows? Are you blocking retries, reconciling, or escalating to a human?
